rv.q: If 'The Moors' sometimes has the discouraging effect of new chalk squeaking across a blackboard, what it ultimately spells out is worth reading.
The fault is in the conception of the story, which wants to have its camp and eat it too.
But the play keeps sabotaging itself.
The Moors delights with its insightful and subversive edginess, toppling the male-oppressed milieus of the Brontës and taking strong, passionate female characters to new heights.
The production’s blend of witty absurdism, boisterous humor, and an unsettling whiff of the macabre sweeps the audience along while always keeping something unexpected around the corner.
Honestly, I can't do better than that.
The Playwrights Realm’s staging of The Moors is a failure that might have been avoided...
Ultimately, this wildly entertaining play also manages to say something profound about human nature, social change, and, yes, the power of writing.

It is this unwillingness of the characters to acknowledge the obvious realities before them -- or perhaps Emilie’s unwillingness to go along with their fantasy -- that lends The Moors its special blend of humor and eeriness.
On the other hand, despite its excellent ensemble—Huppuch is especially noteworthy—others will, like me, find it an overlong, cerebral exercise lacking in emotional warmth and consistent interest.
The direction by Mike Donahue, just draws this whole piece out and in the end it is the audience who is lost on these moors.

cn.t: Silverman's Brontë-inspired dark comedy draws mixed reactions: some find it a clever, entertaining feminist spoof of Gothic conventions, while others criticize it as a promising but unfocused misfire that fails to fully satirize its literary targets.
